content: Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI General, often expert, and sometimes jagged Ethan Mollick Nov 09, 2026 1,485 245 175 Share Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here . I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers. So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: “I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this.” Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end. This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI. The “G” in AGI Code and video creation have been areas where AI development has focused, so is Fable 5.2 really a General Intelligence? To test that, I gave the AI a variety of hard challenges in different domains: Hack some hardware from a single prompt: I have a tiny USB keyboard with a few light-up keys on my desk called a Codex Micro (ironically built to work with ChatGPT), and I asked Fable to turn it into a game console. title: <![CDATA[30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts)]]>
summary: My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite love...
content: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) My new book is out today... what happened since the last one Ethan Mollick Oct 20, 2026 819 148 70 Share My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.” Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. Notice that it corrected me. “This is the worst AI you will ever use” I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence , and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI. Which company had the best AI model in the world. But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone. We are living in an exponential The data below draws on the METR Long Horizon Benchmark, which used to be the most famous chart in AI. The benchmark measured the amount of human work that an AI can do with at least a 50% chance of success from a single prompt. Gains on this benchmark have been startlingly regular. F

content: The Dot and the Swarm - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Dot and the Swarm Benefitting from the Bitter Lesson Ethan Mollick Oct 01, 2026 1,408 236 144 Share I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with agents as a manager, deciding how to delegate work to agents and specifying how those agents should be organized. I thought that getting agents to work effectively as a group would take careful construction, akin to building a company, and that this would take time to figure out. Nope. I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI. The Bitter Lesson is everywhere among AI startups and companies adopting AI. A huge amount of effort went into building elaborate computer systems to feed AIs the right information at the right time, but AI systems have learned to seek out information themselves. The same thing happened to prompting. People built elaborate templates and chains of prompts that walked the AI through a task one step at a time. Then newer models turned out to be better at planning the steps themselves, and, as our research shows , planning steps have much less value. The history of the Bitter Le— — you know what? I don’t really need to explain the Bitter Lesson, I asked Claude to do it in a music video. With one prompt, Fable wrote the lyrics and submitted it to Suno; Opus 5.5 did everything else using code alone without any image generation (How did Opus 5.5 pull this off? The Bitter Lesson tells you!). I gave no feedback at all. As somebody who teaches managers and has published research on management, I guess I believed that managing agents would be different. Humans have been working on management for a very long time without fully figuring it out. It seemed like the kind of thing that would need to be designed by people, at least for a while. It turns out that organizing work is just one more thing AI can learn to do. Which brings us to dots and Muse. Dots and Muse The number one app in the App Store right now is Meta’s Muse, a personal agent that promises to do work for you. OpenAI has now released a competitor tool, called dots. They aren’t alone: SpaceX’s Grok Bot, Instinct, and Gemini Spark all do similar things, more or less. All of these agents draw inspiration from a phenomenon you might remember from earlier this year, OpenClaw. The idea of OpenClaw and its successors, which I will call Clawlikes, is that they give an AI agent access to a computer and connect to your accounts (emails, financial records, etc.). content: My wife thinks AI is a person - Ben's Bites Ben’s Bites Subscribe Sign in My wife thinks AI is a person which isn’t as nuts as it sounds... Nov 19, 2026 43 Share The other day my wife was chatting with AI. P.s. The full interactive version of this post is here . So let’s overlook the actual impossibilities and find out. Before we do the maths, people have been trying versions of this for 256 years. Nearly all of them shut down or got caught. None of them came close to today’s scale. So what would it actually take? Let’s be generous. Assume everyone types at world-record speed, 200 words a minute, non-stop. Everyone is happy to wait 10 minutes for a reply. And it’s a remote company spread across every time zone, so someone is always awake. The average ChatGPT user sends about 4 messages a day, and a reply is roughly 500 words now. With over a billion people using the big AI chatbots, that’s about 6 billion messages every day. 10.4 million people typing at world-record speed, round the clock, with no sleep, no lunch, and no days off. Okay, let’s run it like a real company instead. Which means it needs a CEO. Me. 11.8 billion internal messages a day, just to keep the place running. Oh, and we still have to answer the 6 billion messages people actually sent us. All in, you’d need 77.4 million staff just to keep 10.4 million people typing at any given moment. If you want to check my maths: a 40-hour week, time off from a 2025 survey of UK call centres , 12.1 people per manager ( the US average ), and 2 HR people per 100 staff ( SHRM ). People quit at the US rate , earn the US median for customer service , and get 153 chat messages a day , like the average Microsoft Teams user. The biggest Zoom call holds 1 million . More people won’t work. But what about a guessing game from 1950, played by a mathematician called Claude Shannon? Yes, Claude. He picked a line from a book, hid it from his wife Betty, and got her to guess it one letter at a time. Betty didn’t know the sentence, she just knew the patterns of English. My wife does this to me every day. She’s had years of practice. So what if we replaced Betty with a computer? For more than 60 years, the answer was no. Giving machines more to read barely helped, because they could only see the last couple of words. Try guessing what comes after “speak fluent…” with no other clues. In 2017, eight people at Google let it see every word at once and weigh the ones that matter, like France. They called that attention, and the machine a transformer. It’s the T in ChatGPT. Suddenly, giving it more to read actually worked. More text, bigger brain, better guesses. Writing a reply is the same thing. It reads what you said and guesses the next word, or piece of a word (called a token), sticks it on the end, looks back at everything again, and guesses the next one. content: Productiv-icky - by Ben Tossell - Ben's Bites Ben’s Bites Subscribe Sign in Productiv-icky Digging holes on the beach Ben Tossell Nov 17, 2026 77 4 1 Share productiv-icky (adj.) - the feeling of doing work you didn’t mean to do We have a problem. full interactive post is here We agree this is insane, right? Someone I don’t know sends me emails that I’m expected to reply to. I don’t know them. I don’t work for them. So I ignore them (well actually I send them to email jail). Nuh-uh, that’s not my work, buddy. But it’s different if it’s my super-intelligent, helpful agent friend… Yeses are easy. They’re quick. But every yes has a yes-tax. The hidden extra work you didn’t think of. The long tail of regret where you question why you ever said yes. Say I did reply to those emails, they’d send me stuff to read to show how great they are at their job and how much better I’d be. Then we’d organise a call (which would derail whichever day that call was on). Then we’d have follow-up items. Then a string of other crap I couldn’t care less about. I know what’s going to happen. I can smell it, it stinks. I’ve said yes and paid the tax many times before. Now I pay $200/mo for a super-intelligent, over-eager, needy little nerd to ping me incessantly about taking things off my plate. I feel bad for him. He wants to work. He’s gagging for it. Just. One. More. Task. Master. Plus, my little nerd has a gambling problem. Or rather, he feeds mine. Remember years ago sending tons of Slack messages to get the most out of your $20/mo plan? Nor me. Why? Because it’s dumb. But now we feel like we should use all our tokens before they run out. Why? Because everyone else is. We started measuring shovels instead of the hole. Someone’s needy little nerd booked their dentist, replied to their mum and launched a business whilst they were asleep. They’ve got an org chart. For nerds. With a Chief of Staff. You feel behind. Like way behind. So you grab a shovel and start digging. A little hole over there to triage your inbox, one here to draft your tweets, one to check on those. Then you spend your day checking the holes are being dug right. Before long, you’re surrounded by holes and a mountain of dirt you gotta do something with. Now as a man, holes are hardwired into my DNA. A few beers, a beach and a shovel, I’m digging a hole. I’d take pride in it. I’d make the best one, impressively round, deep enough to see sea water seep through the bottom. But I’d only dig one. There’s a whole beach but I chose this spot. Next time the needy little nerd pings you: do you really want another hole? Also, don’t dig big holes on the beach. They collapse. content: To the man with AI, everything looks like a task Ben’s Bites Subscribe Sign in To the man with AI, everything looks like a task Real* quote from Charlie Munger - lightly modernised :) Ben Tossell Nov 12, 2026 45 9 3 Share Now I’m having fun! My Ramp post was really well received with one or two ‘I’m not sure what I just looked at’ comments (which is totally fair). The best I can describe what I’m doing now is exploring people and companies who are having fun with AI, doing things differently, being authentic and succeeding . Which is basically how I want to describe my ‘work’. But I think a lot of people are living in fear. Scared they’re behind, they’re not doing enough, others using AI ‘better’ than them, where’s there job going etc. I want to focus on using AI for fun. AI is a tool, you need one agent app (I’ve been using Droid with Opus 5.5 medium, fast mode for my posts, fable here and there). Use the tool to do work beyond what you could do before, don’t think about how you can finally optimise every aspect of every little thing. (I’ve basically stopped using Grok Bot, except telling me when the tennis is on). As part of my explorations I’m working on a new post for another company I admire and who do things very differently. Coming next week… “Everyone judges a book by its cover” Can you guess which company it is? And yes, these animations are staying. Honestly I love them. I love making them too. So much so that I set up a sophisticated camera set up to monitor what my days look like and here’s the footage. Morning voice dump. Kids. Stickmen. Adobe Firefly, the AI creative studio , lets you describe what you want to create, then review the Adobe Creative Agent’s plan before it gets to work using Creative Cloud tools. You stay in control from first idea to finished result. Try it today in the Firefly Assistant! * Quick bites Anthropic is building all office software inside Claude. Latest addition: whiteboards, sheets and data . Meetings soon? Gemini 4 Carbon is out for Ultra subscribers and in the API. Also see: Gemini Decision 1 (Google’s Jev-like model) Grok Bot is now in Slack, Teams and your video calls. You can now claim your business in ChatGPT and see how often it gets mentioned. Granola now writes a nightly Agent Brief about you that any agent can read. Practical Data colours any table on the web so you can see what’s good and bad at a glance. Karri Saarinen @ karrisaarinen give a man a tool, and he'll get to work. give a man a way to build his own tools, and building tools becomes his work. 9:56 PM · Nov 11, 2026 · 26.1K Views 48 Replies · 70 Reposts · 832 Likes Jason Dainter @ jasondainter 99% AI. title: <![CDATA[Open-source AI without Jensen]]>
summary: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s p...
content: Open-source AI without Jensen - by Nathan Lambert Subscribe Sign in Open-source AI without Jensen A decapitation. It’s time to rebuild. Nathan Lambert Nov 14, 2026 121 24 20 Share Article voiceover 0:00 -7:28 Audio playback is not supported on your browser. Please upgrade. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on. Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up. Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Subscribe In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ( slides , recording ). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside. The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is. The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy . Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine.
